blocks.text: **The task.** Rotate an N x N matrix 90 degrees clockwise, modifying it in place with O(1) extra space.
Study the result and the rule emerges: the first **row** becomes the last **column**, the second row becomes the second-to-last column.

You could allocate a new matrix and place each element directly. That is O(N²) space, and the problem forbids it. Doing it in place with direct swaps means chasing four-element cycles — correct but painful to get right.
The trick: compose two easy operations
A 90° clockwise rotation equals a **transpose** followed by a **horizontal reflection of each row**. Both are simple and both are in place.
Why the inner loop starts at r + 1
Transposing swaps `(r,c)` with `(c,r)`. Starting the inner loop at 0 would visit each pair **twice** — once as `(r,c)` and once as `(c,r)` — swapping them back and leaving the matrix unchanged.
Starting at `r + 1` visits only the upper triangle, so each pair is swapped exactly once. The diagonal itself is skipped because `(r,r)` swaps with itself.
Reverse the order of the two steps: reverse each row **first**, then transpose. Same two operations, opposite direction.
**Time: O(N²)** — every element is touched a constant number of times.
The lesson generalises: a transformation that is awkward directly is often the composition of two that are not.
